items.rationalization: Juncture indicates the phonetic transition between syllables or words, signaling boundary distinctions between lexical elements in connected speech.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What term designates the lack of any real pause or break between the syllables of words?
items.rationalization: Close juncture occurs when sound segments transition into one another without an acoustic break, as seen within seamless single words.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What type of juncture describes an audible break or pause between syllables in adjacent words, as in 'night rate' versus 'nitrate'?
items.rationalization: Open (plus) juncture creates the distinct acoustic boundary separating words, allowing listeners to differentiate pairs like 'night rate' from 'nitrate'.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which phonetic contrast is illustrated by 'why try' versus 'white rye'?
items.rationalization: The timing and boundary transitions of the consonant and vowel sequences distinguish 'why try' from 'white rye', serving as an example of juncture.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What are the three definitive criteria that a language segment must meet to be classified as a morpheme?
items.definition: It is a meaningful word/part, cannot be divided without violating meaning or leaving meaningless remainders, and recurs with relatively stable meaning.
items.rationalization: A morpheme is the minimal meaningful grammatical unit; dividing it further yields either non-meaningful remnants or unrelated semantic components.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: How many morphemes constitute the word 'unhappiness' according to morphological analysis?
items.rationalization: 'Unhappiness' consists of the prefix {un-}, the free base root {happy}, and the noun-forming suffix {-ness}.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Why is the word 'salamander' analyzed as containing only a single morpheme?
items.definition: It cannot be divided into smaller meaningful parts without violation of its meaning or leaving meaningless remainders.
items.rationalization: Subdividing 'salamander' (e.g., into 'sala' and 'mander') leaves meaningless strings that do not recur with stable semantic content.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What are allomorphs?
items.definition: Phonologically or morphologically conditioned morph variants that belong to the same morpheme.
items.rationalization: Allomorphs represent positional or structural variants of a single underlying morpheme, such as the predictable variants of the English plural.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which phonological variants represent the allomorphs of the regular plural morpheme {(e)s} in 'cats', 'bags', and 'buses'?
items.rationalization: The regular plural morpheme surfaces as voiceless /s/ after voiceless stops, voiced /z/ after voiced consonants/vowels, and /əz/ after sibilants.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: In the irregular plural nouns 'oxen' and 'children', what suffix serves as an allomorph of the plural morpheme?
items.rationalization: The suffix {-en} is a morphologically conditioned allomorph of the English plural morpheme {plural}.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What is the defining characteristic of a free morpheme?
items.definition: It can stand on its own as an independent word and occur in isolation.
items.rationalization: Free morphemes like 'happy', 'like', and 'boy' can occur independently in syntax without requiring accompanying bound affixes.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What is the defining characteristic of a bound morpheme?
items.definition: It cannot stand on its own as an independent word and must attach to another morpheme.
items.rationalization: Bound morphemes, including prefixes and suffixes like {un-}, {-ly}, and {-hood}, only surface attached to base stems or roots.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: In the words 'conceive', 'deceive', and 'perceive', what type of bound morphemes are 'con-', 'de-', and 'per-'?
items.definition: Bound morphemes (bound prefixes) attached to a bound root ({-ceive}).
items.rationalization: The prefixes {con-}, {de-}, and {per-} are bound morphemes that combine with the bound Latinate root {-ceive}.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What is an inflectional morpheme?
items.definition: A morpheme that attaches to complete words to express grammatical relations without changing their form class.
items.rationalization: Inflectional morphemes mark grammatical functions such as tense, aspect, or number without altering the lexical part of speech or core semantic category.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: How many inflectional morphemes exist in the English language?
items.rationalization: English maintains a strictly closed set of eight inflectional affixes, all of which are suffixes.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which English inflectional morpheme is exemplified in 'She stays at home'?
items.rationalization: The suffix '-s' added to the verb 'stay' marks agreement with a third-person singular subject in the present tense.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which English inflectional morpheme appears in 'She stayed at home'?
items.rationalization: The suffix '-ed' attaches to regular verbs to indicate past tense.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What inflectional morpheme is marked in 'She is staying at home'?
items.rationalization: The verbal affix '-ing' marks progressive aspect when paired with an auxiliary 'be' verb.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which inflectional morpheme is demonstrated in 'She has eaten at home'?
items.rationalization: The affix '-en' is the inflectional marker indicating the past participial form of irregular verbs like 'eat'.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What inflectional morpheme occurs in the phrase 'She wrote novels'?
items.rationalization: The suffix '-s' inflects the noun 'novel' to mark nominal plural number.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: In 'Marie's car is new', which English inflectional morpheme is attached to the noun?
items.rationalization: The affix "-'s" is the English inflectional marker expressing possession or genitive case on noun phrases.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which inflectional morpheme is illustrated in 'This road is longer than that'?
items.rationalization: The suffix '-er' attaches to gradable adjectives to form the comparative degree.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which inflectional morpheme is illustrated in 'This is the longest road'?
items.rationalization: The inflectional suffix '-est' marks the superlative degree of an adjective.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Why are inflectional morphemes said to 'cap' a word?
items.definition: No other affixes can be added to a word after an inflectional affix is attached.
items.rationalization: Inflectional morphemes close the word to further derivational affixation; they always occur outside derivational affixes at the very edge of the base.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What is a derivational morpheme?
items.definition: An affix added to roots or stems that derives new words and usually changes their syntactic category.
items.rationalization: Derivational morphemes create new lexical items (e.g., 'actual' -> 'actualize') and represent an open-ended, potentially infinite inventory.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What morphological process is illustrated by adding {-ize} to 'actual' to produce 'actualize'?
items.rationalization: Derivation involves attaching an affix to change the syntactic category or core lexical meaning of a base (here, adjective to verb).
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What word-formation process is demonstrated when 'discern' (V) becomes 'discernment' (N)?
items.rationalization: The addition of the derivational suffix '-ment' alters the verb into a noun, exemplifying derivational morphology.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What word-formation process occurs when 'woman' (N) becomes 'womanly' (Adj)?
items.rationalization: Adding the derivational suffix '-ly' shifts the noun 'woman' into the adjective 'womanly'.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What word-formation process extends a morpheme from one syntactic category to another without adding an affix, as in 'house' (N) becoming 'house' (V)?
items.rationalization: Category extension (also known as conversion or functional shift) shifts a word into a new part of speech without any overt morphological alteration.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: The shift of 'fast' from an adjective ('a fast runner') to an adverb ('he runs fast') exemplifies which word-formation process?
items.rationalization: Because the lexical shape remains unchanged while its syntactic category expands from adjective to adverb, it represents category extension.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What word-formation process creates a new word by combining two free morphemes, such as 'sunset' or 'drugstore'?
items.rationalization: Compounding joins two independent free morphemes together to yield a single lexical item.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What word-formation process creates a brand new word based on no pre-existing morphemes, such as 'Colgate' or 'Xerox'?
items.rationalization: Root creation produces entirely novel coinages or trademark brand names without combining or modifying pre-existing morphemes.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What word-formation process produces 'gym' from 'gymnasium' and 'mike' from 'microphone'?
items.rationalization: Clipping shortens a polysyllabic pre-existing form while retaining its original semantic meaning and syntactic category.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What word-formation process combines parts of two pre-existing forms, as seen in 'smog' (smoke + fog) and 'motel' (motor + hotel)?
items.rationalization: A blend is formed by fusing non-morphemic pieces of two distinct words together into a single combined form.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What word-formation process forms a word from the initial letters of each word in a phrase and is pronounced as a single word, such as 'NASA' and 'SARS'?
items.rationalization: Acronyms are formed from the initial letter(s) of constituent words in a multi-word title or phrase and pronounced phonetically as an ordinary word.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: How does the source distinguish an 'abbreviation' like 'TV' or 'FBI' from an 'acronym'?
items.definition: An abbreviation is formed from the names of the letters spoken individually rather than pronounced as a word.
items.rationalization: Abbreviation (initialism) involves pronouncing the names of the prominent letters in sequence (e.g., /t/ /v/), whereas acronyms are pronounced as ordinary words (e.g., NASA).
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What word-formation process is responsible for words like 'hamburger' (from Hamburg) and 'sandwich' (from Earl of Sandwich)?
items.rationalization: This process shifts a specific proper noun (such as a geographic location or historical person) into a common noun.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What word-formation process substitutes a common native form for an unfamiliar foreign form, as in 'cockroach' from Spanish 'cucuracha'?
items.rationalization: Folk etymology reanalyzes and replaces exotic or opaque borrowed phonetic sequences with familiar native morphological elements.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What word-formation process forms 'edit' from 'editor' and 'beg' from 'beggar'?
items.rationalization: Back formation creates a new base word by removing an affix-like segment mistakenly analyzed as an actual derivational suffix.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What morphophonemic process causes a sound to take on phonetic characteristics of a neighboring sound?
items.rationalization: Assimilation increases phonetic similarity between adjacent segments, as when the alveolar nasal in 'in-' becomes bilabial 'im-' before bilabials.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: The shifts in prefixes seen in 'improbable', 'impotent', 'inseparable', and 'insensitive' illustrate which morphophonemic process?
items.rationalization: The negative prefix /ɪn-/ assimilates its place of articulation to bilabial [m] before /p/ in 'improbable' and remains alveolar [n] before alveolar /s/ in 'insensitive'.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What morphophonemic process causes two nearby sounds to become less alike or causes one of them to be lost?
items.rationalization: Dissimilation occurs when identical or similar acoustic features in close proximity become differentiated or deleted to facilitate articulation.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Pronouncing 'library' as 'libary' or 'governor' as 'govenor' illustrates which morphophonemic process?
items.rationalization: One of two closely occurring /r/ sounds is dropped, reducing the articulatory repetition of identical liquid consonants.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What morphophonemic process removes a sound segment from certain phonetic environments in rapid speech?
items.rationalization: Deletion eliminates an underlying segment, such as dropping the final /d/ in rapid pronunciation of 'blind man'.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Pronouncing 'blind man' as [blaɪn mæn] is an example of which morphophonemic process?
items.rationalization: The alveolar stop /d/ at the coda of 'blind' is completely omitted in fluent speech before the nasal /m/.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What morphophonemic process inserts an extra segment or syllable into an existing string of sounds?
items.rationalization: Epenthesis inserts an intrusive vowel or consonant segment, such as inserting the vowel [ɪ] when pronouncing 'planted' [plæntɪd].
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: The pronunciation of 'planted' as [plæntɪd] with an inserted vowel illustrates which morphophonemic process?
items.rationalization: The insertion of the lax vowel [ɪ] between the root-final alveolar stop /t/ and the past-tense suffix /d/ exemplifies epenthesis.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What morphophonemic process reorders or switches the sequence of two segments in a word?
items.rationalization: Metathesis transposes the linear order of adjacent or nearby speech sounds within a word.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Pronouncing 'ask' as 'aks', 'ruler' as 'lurer', or 'violet' as 'viloyet' exemplifies which linguistic process?
items.rationalization: These examples show adjacent or nearby consonants/vowels switching linear positions within the word string.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which syntactic structure consists of two basic components: a subject and a predicate?
items.rationalization: A structure of predication unites a noun phrase subject with a verb phrase predicate that makes an assertion about that subject.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Phrases like 'the seagull flies', 'the water level rose abruptly', and 'the trial has begun' represent which syntactic structure?
items.rationalization: Each example links an overt subject noun phrase with a functioning verbal predicate asserting an action or state.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which syntactic structure consists of a verbal element and a complement?
items.rationalization: Structures of complementation combine a transitive, linking, or predicating verb with its required complement.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Verb phrases such as 'disturbed the class', 'rendered service', and 'be conscientious' exemplify which syntactic structure?
items.rationalization: Each phrase consists of a verbal head followed by an object or predicative complement completing its syntactic requirement.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which syntactic structure contains a head word and a modifier that serves to broaden, qualify, or describe it?
items.rationalization: In modification structures, a head word's meaning is selected, restricted, or qualified by an attributive modifier.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Phrases like 'responsible officers', 'trusted friend', and 'impartially conducted' represent which syntactic structure?
items.rationalization: Each phrase pairs a head noun or verb with an adjectival or adverbial modifier that qualifies its meaning.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which syntactic structure consists of equivalent grammatical units joined often by a coordinating conjunction?
items.rationalization: Structures of coordination link two or more constituents of identical grammatical status, typically using conjunctions like 'and', 'but', or correlatives.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: The phrases 'bread and butter', 'peace not war', and 'neither extrovert nor introvert' are examples of which syntactic structure?
items.rationalization: Each phrase links syntactically parallel phrases using coordinating or correlative elements.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What semantic phenomenon occurs when a single lexical word has more than one meaning or sense?
items.rationalization: Lexical ambiguity arises at word level when an individual word form maps onto multiple distinct meanings.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Why is the word 'fly' cited in semantics as an example of lexical ambiguity?
items.definition: It can mean an insect, a zipper on pants, or a baseball hit high in the air.
items.rationalization: The single phonetic and orthographic form 'fly' carries several completely distinct semantic definitions.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What semantic condition occurs when an entire phrase has more than one meaning due to multiple possible structural interpretations?
items.rationalization: Syntactic (structural) ambiguity stems from differing constituent groupings rather than multiple senses of an isolated word.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: How does the phrase 'English literature teacher' demonstrate syntactic ambiguity?
items.definition: It can mean a teacher who teaches English literature or a literature teacher who comes from England.
items.rationalization: The phrase allows two internal bracketings: [English literature] teacher versus English [literature teacher].
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: In semantics, what relation holds between words that have identical values for all their semantic features?
items.rationalization: Synonyms share identical semantic feature specifications, rendering their core cognitive senses equivalent.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: The word pairs 'happy / glad', 'reply / respond', and 'hastily / hurriedly' exemplify which semantic relationship?
items.rationalization: Each pair consists of distinct words that share the same semantic sense and feature values.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What is hyponymy in lexical semantics?
items.definition: A sense relation where the meaning of a specific word is included in the broader meaning of a superordinate word.
items.rationalization: A hyponym shares all semantic features of its superordinate term plus additional specific feature values.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: In the relationship between 'sampaguita' and 'flower', what technical semantic term designates 'sampaguita'?
items.rationalization: 'Sampaguita' is the subordinate member (hyponym) whose semantic specification incorporates the broader category 'flower'.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: In the semantic relationship between 'sampaguita' and 'flower', what technical term identifies 'flower'?
items.rationalization: The containing, broader taxonomic class is termed the superordinate (or hypernym).
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What semantic relation describes two words that differ in form and express opposite senses?
items.rationalization: Antonyms convey polar or contrasting semantic senses, often differing across the value of a single binary feature.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: How are binary antonyms like 'dead / alive' analyzed in terms of semantic features?
items.definition: They differ only in the value of a single semantic feature (e.g., dead is [-life] and alive is [+life]).
items.rationalization: Binary (complementary) antonyms are non-gradable; affirming one necessarily negates the other along a single binary parameter.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: How do gradable antonyms like 'hot' and 'cold' differ from binary antonyms?
items.definition: They represent opposite ends of a continuous dimension with intermediate degrees (e.g., warm or cool).
items.rationalization: Gradable antonyms do not represent absolute either/or choices; they allow for intermediate states along an acoustic or physical scale.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What semantic relation occurs when two words share the same phonetic form but possess entirely unrelated meanings?
items.rationalization: Homonyms are distinct lexical entries that happen to have identical phonological shapes, having separate meanings.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: The word 'bat' (a flying nocturnal animal) and 'bat' (baseball equipment) illustrate which semantic relation?
items.rationalization: Because both words share identical phonetic and orthographic forms without sharing underlying semantic origin, they are homonyms.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What semantic relation exists between two distinct expressions that pick out the identical real-world entity?
items.rationalization: Coreference occurs when two different nominal expressions share the same extralinguistic referent in the world.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: In 'Mercury is the nearest planet from the sun', why are 'Mercury' and 'the nearest planet from the sun' coreferential?
items.definition: Both expressions point to the identical extralinguistic object in reality.
items.rationalization: The proper noun and the descriptive noun phrase point to the identical astronomical body.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What is anaphora in linguistic analysis?
items.definition: A relation where a linguistic expression points backward to derive its interpretation from a preceding expression.
items.rationalization: An anaphor relies on an antecedent earlier in the discourse to establish its semantic interpretation.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: In 'The tsunami killed thousands of people. It was devastating', how is the pronoun 'It' functioning?
items.definition: Anaphorically, pointing backwards to refer to 'the tsunami'.
items.rationalization: The pronoun 'It' acts as an anaphor whose referent is provided by the antecedent noun phrase 'the tsunami'.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What linguistic property describes expressions that have a stable meaning but refer to different entities depending on the context of utterance?
items.rationalization: Deictic expressions serve a 'pointing function' whose actual referents shift depending on who speaks, where, and when.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Personal pronouns such as 'I', 'you', and 'she' belong to which functional category of reference?
items.rationalization: Pronouns depend directly on participant roles in the communicative event, embodying the pointing function of deixis.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Spatial adverbs like 'here' and 'there' and demonstratives like 'this' and 'that' illustrate which linguistic property?
items.rationalization: These terms locate entities relative to the physical position of the speaker at the time of utterance.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Temporal expressions such as 'now', 'yesterday', 'today', and 'last year' exemplify which linguistic category?
items.rationalization: Time deixis anchors reference points relative to the exact moment the utterance is produced.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What is an entailment in semantics?
items.definition: A proposition expressed in a sentence that follows necessarily from another sentence.
items.rationalization: Entailment is a strict truth-conditional relation: if sentence A is true, sentence B must unavoidably and necessarily be true.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: According to the vowel chart from Parker and Riley, which vowel phonemes are classified as English front vowels?
items.rationalization: The front vowel series in English spans from high front /i/ down to low front /æ/.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: According to Parker and Riley's vowel chart, which vowel phonemes represent the back vowels of English?
items.rationalization: English back and central-back vowels mapped in the chart include high /u, ℧/, mid /o, Λ, ә, Ɔ/, and low /a/.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: In English vowel classification, what articulatory dimension differentiates /i/ from /ɪ/?
items.rationalization: Both /i/ and /ɪ/ are high front unrounded vowels, but /i/ is tense while /ɪ/ is lax.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: In English phonetics, how is the vowel /u/ classified compared to /℧/?
items.rationalization: Both vowels are high back rounded vowels, distinguished primarily by muscle tension and duration: /u/ is tense, /℧/ is lax.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which lip configuration characterizes front vowels in the Parker and Riley chart?
items.rationalization: Front vowels in English are articulated with spread or neutral lip positions, unlike the rounded back vowels.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which lip configuration characterizes non-low back vowels such as /u/, /℧/, and /o/?
items.rationalization: Non-low English back vowels are produced with protruding, rounded lips.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What vowel height classification applies to the phonemes /æ/ and /a/?
items.rationalization: In the English vowel quadrilateral, /æ/ (front) and /a/ (back) are articulated with the tongue body in the lowest position.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which vowel height classification encompasses /e/, /ε/, /o/, /Λ/, and /Ɔ/?
items.rationalization: These phonemes occupy the intermediate vertical tier between the high vowels (/i, ɪ, u, ℧/) and low vowels (/æ, a/).
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which front mid vowel is categorized as tense in the Parker and Riley chart?
items.rationalization: The vowel /e/ is classified as a mid front tense vowel, while /ε/ is mid front lax.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What is the tense/lax status of the mid front vowel /ε/?
items.rationalization: The vowel /ε/ (as in 'bed') is articulated with less muscular constriction, classifying it as lax.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: True or False: Derivational affixes represent a closed-ended set in English.
items.definition: False; derivational affixes are open-ended and potentially infinite, whereas inflectional morphemes are a closed set of eight.
items.rationalization: Derivational morphemes can be coined and expanded continuously, unlike the strictly limited inventory of eight English inflectional morphemes.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: True or False: Inflectional morphemes can change the grammatical category of the word to which they attach.
items.definition: False; inflectional morphemes never change the form class of the base word.
items.rationalization: Inflections modify grammatical features like tense or number; only derivational morphemes alter grammatical category.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: In semantics, what other technical term is used interchangeably with 'entailment' when the meaning of one sentence includes the meaning of another?
items.rationalization: The source material specifies that when the meaning of a first sentence includes the meaning of the second, it is called an entailment or a paraphrase. Presupposition refers to a proposition assumed to be true beforehand, while implicature refers to an implied meaning that is not a necessary consequence.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Why does the sentence 'Raul had a fatal accident' semantically entail that 'Raul died'?
items.definition: Because 'fatal' contains the semantic feature [-life] and 'died' also contains [-life], making it impossible to have a fatal accident without loss of life.
items.rationalization: Entailment holds because the semantic component [-life] in 'fatal' strictly necessitates the [-life] meaning of 'died'. If a person survives, the accident cannot truthfully be characterized as fatal.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What semantic feature is shared by both 'fatal' and 'died' in the entailment 'Raul had a fatal accident entails Raul died'?
items.rationalization: According to the source, semantically speaking, both 'fatal' and 'died' carry the feature [-life]. This shared semantic feature guarantees that the truth of the first statement logically requires the truth of the second.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What is defined in semantics as a proposition expressed in a sentence that is assumed to be true in order to judge the truth or falsity of another sentence?
items.rationalization: Presupposition refers to background assumptions taken for granted in an utterance. If the presupposition is false, the main sentence cannot be assigned a valid truth value (it lacks a truth value).
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Under what condition does one sentence presuppose another sentence in semantic truth relations?
items.definition: When the falsity of the second sentence renders the first sentence without a truth value.
items.rationalization: In semantic theory, presupposition is distinguished by truth failure: if the presupposed statement is false, the asserting statement is neither true nor false (it lacks a truth value entirely). In contrast, if an entailed sentence is false, the entailing sentence is simply false.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What does the sentence 'The King of Canada is dead' presuppose?
items.definition: There exists (is) a King of Canada.
items.rationalization: The existence of a King of Canada is the necessary background assumption. If no King of Canada exists, the statement 'The King of Canada is dead' cannot be judged as either true or false; it lacks a truth value.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Why does the statement 'The King of Canada is dead' lack a truth value if there is no King of Canada?
items.definition: Because the presupposed proposition ('There exists a King of Canada') is false, which deprives the assertion of a truth value.
items.rationalization: Presupposition failure results in truth-value gaps; an utterance whose fundamental presupposition is false cannot be evaluated as true or false. Entailment failure merely results in falsity, not the absence of a truth value.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which linguistic theory asserts that every utterance of speech constitutes some sort of act such as promising, apologizing, threatening, or warning?
items.rationalization: Speech act theory, originally formulated by J.L. Austin and expanded by John Searle, treats utterances as functional actions rather than mere grammatical strings. Discourse analysis and conversational implicature deal with broader communicative interactions and implied meanings.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: According to Speech Act Theory, what three separate acts constitute every speech act?
items.definition: Locutionary act (force), illocutionary act (force), and perlocutionary act
items.rationalization: Every complete speech act encompasses the physical act of speaking (locution), the conventional social intent of the speaker (illocution), and the resulting effect upon the addressee (perlocution).
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: How is the 'locutionary force' or 'locutionary act' defined in speech act theory?
items.definition: The act of saying something; a description of what a speaker says.
items.rationalization: The locutionary act refers to the literal, linguistic production of words and sounds that carry grammatical and semantic form. The illocutionary act is the intended function, and the perlocutionary act is the resulting effect.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: In the utterance 'I promise to return your book tomorrow', what constitutes the locutionary act?
items.definition: The literal act of uttering the words 'I promise to return your book tomorrow'.
items.rationalization: The locutionary dimension is solely the physical and verbal articulation of the sentence. The act of binding oneself to return the book is the illocutionary force.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What is the 'illocutionary act' or 'illocutionary force' in speech act theory?
items.definition: The act of doing something; what the speaker intends to do by uttering a sentence.
items.rationalization: Illocutionary force embodies the speaker's communicative intent or purpose, such as promising, demanding, or greeting. Locution is the saying, whereas illocution is the doing accomplished through saying.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: When a speaker utters 'I promise to return your book tomorrow', what illocutionary act has been performed?
items.rationalization: The speaker explicitly commits to a future course of action, which constitutes the illocutionary act of making a promise. The listener's subsequent feelings represent the perlocutionary outcome.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What is a 'perlocutionary act' in speech act theory?
items.definition: An act of affecting someone (i.e., the listener); the effect on the hearer of what a speaker says.
items.rationalization: A perlocutionary act concerns the actual psychological or behavioral consequences produced in the hearer (e.g., persuasion, fright, relief). It is not strictly within the speaker's total linguistic control.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: If a speaker says 'I will return your book tomorrow' and the hearer feels happy or relieved, what speech act component does this emotional reaction represent?
items.rationalization: The hearer's feeling of happiness or relief is the consequential effect of the utterance, which defines the perlocutionary dimension. The locution is the verbal statement, and the illocution is the commitment/promise.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Which philosopher and linguist proposed the categories used to group together closely related intentions in illocutionary acts?
items.rationalization: John Searle systematized J.L. Austin's initial speech act framework into well-defined illocutionary categories including declarations, representatives, commissives, directives, expressives, and questions.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What category of illocutionary act is defined as an utterance used to change the status of some entity?
items.rationalization: Declarations immediately alter the external institutional or social reality once uttered by an authorized person in an appropriate context. Representatives describe reality, whereas declarations create a new reality.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: When a referee shouts 'Foul!' at a basketball game, which category of illocutionary act is demonstrated?
items.rationalization: The referee's utterance instantly alters the game state and the player's status within the rules of basketball, making it a declaration. Directives request action, whereas declarations officially enact changes in institutional status.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Acts such as appointing, naming, resigning, baptizing, surrendering, excommunicating, and arresting belong to which class of illocutionary acts?
items.rationalization: All these performative acts immediately establish a new social, legal, or institutional state of affairs. Representatives convey beliefs, whereas declarations perform structural institutional transformations.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What category of illocutionary act is defined as an utterance used to describe some state of affairs?
items.rationalization: Representatives commit the speaker to the truth of the expressed proposition and convey statements, claims, or hypotheses about the world. Commissives commit the speaker to future actions instead.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: The statement 'Recession will worsen in Europe in the next five years' is an example of which illocutionary act?
items.rationalization: This utterance describes or predicts a state of affairs in the world, matching the definition of a representative. It is not an expressive because it states a claim rather than expressing an emotional state.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: Acts of stating, asserting, denying, confessing, admitting, notifying, concluding, and predicting belong to which illocutionary category?
items.rationalization: These verbs convey the speaker's belief or description regarding facts and states of affairs. Declarations change an institutional state, while representatives represent how things are or will be.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: What category of illocutionary act is defined as an utterance used to commit the speaker to do something?
items.rationalization: Commissives bind the speaker to a prospective future course of action (e.g., promising, pledging). Directives attempt to get the hearer to act, whereas commissives commit the speaker.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics

items.term: The utterance 'I'll meet you at the library at 10:00 a.m.' exemplifies which category of illocutionary act?
items.rationalization: The speaker obligates themselves to be present at the library at a designated time, constituting a commissive. A directive would instruct the hearer to meet there instead.
items.tosCompetency: Demonstrate understanding of the nature of language and the core areas of linguistics
